papers.abstract: Solar flares are the most energetic impulsive events in the solar system, and reliable operational forecasting of the rarest and most destructive M- and X-class events remains an open problem. We present Solar Heliospherical Analysis and Prediction of Eruptions (SHAPE), a two-phase deep-learning pipeline that bypasses sunspot proxies in favour of direct soft X-ray observations from the GOES X-ray Sensor (XRS). Phase 1 forecasts monthly flare counts, aggregated to annual totals, with a hybrid model: a cycle-shape curve anchored to published solar-cycle minima fixes the timing and mean profile, and a compact gated-recurrent-unit network with Monte Carlo dropout models the residual variability. Trained on the science-quality NOAA GOES Flare Report for 1995--2020 and validated on 2021--2025, it achieves a mean absolute error of 204 flares yr$^{-1}$, although it underestimates the 2024 solar maximum. Phase 2 forecasts the next day's strongest flare class (C, M or X) with a shared-trunk, dual-head LSTM operating on a 12-day rolling window of five intensity features, with an optional blend against an active-region physics score and a decision threshold tuned to favour recall of M-or-above (M+) events. On a 100-day chronological backtest, the classifier attains a true skill statistic of 0.351, a Heidke skill score of 0.335 for M+ events, a Brier skill score of 0.163 relative to climatology, and an expected calibration error of 0.023. A day-to-day persistence baseline is, however, competitive on both skill scores, showing that much short-term predictability in flare class is autocorrelation rather than learned structure. SHAPE shows that competitive flare forecasting is achievable with compact architectures that retain in minutes on standard hardware, without sunspot proxy inputs.

papers.title: Specification-Driven Governance for Fairness-by-Design in Agentic Software Engineering: How Far Can We Go?
papers.abstract: Agentic AI is shifting developers' responsibilities from software implementation to software governance. While this paradigm improves productivity, it also raises challenges in ensuring that autonomous coding agents preserve developers' intentions. Among these, operationalizing fairness-by-design is largely unexplored, as existing approaches provide limited support for representing and propagating fairness requirements throughout agentic development workflows. In this paper, we investigate whether specification-driven development can operationalize fairness-by-design in the agentic development of machine learning systems. We study three coding agents on four machine learning applications, using four prompts that progressively operationalize fairness through nine Fairness Specification Elements, and analyze the traceability of fairness requirements across the generated artifacts, the fairness-accuracy trade-off of the resulting models, and the agents' design decisions and rationales. The results show that when fairness is operationalized, agents capture almost all fairness requirements in the specification (97.22%) and preserve most of them in the code (82.41%). However, the resulting models are not significantly fairer, as agents implement fairness as a post-hoc audit that neither shapes training nor prevents model delivery. Specifications thus make fairness traceable, but not enforceable, calling for fairness specifications that state what agents should do when requirements are not met, and for workflows that make the fairness decisions agents delegate to developers explicit.

papers.title: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science
papers.abstract: Machine learning supports materials design, atomistic simulation and experimental characterization, yet models and workflows remain fragmented. We present PaddleMaterials, an open-source framework integrating heterogeneous materials-learning tasks while preserving task-specific representations and scientific semantics. It unifies data processing, training, evaluation, pretrained-model management and workflows across six task classes: property prediction, structure generation, machine-learning interatomic potentials, electronic-structure fields, spectrum elucidation and microscopy image processing. Task interfaces record physical quantities, units, aggregation conventions and references, making cross-task composition verifiable. A shared compiler backend enables switching from dynamic-graph to compiled execution through one setting, using graph optimization, operator fusion and hardware-targeted code generation without changing model definitions. Across 65 model instances in 11 groups, compiled execution accelerated every instance in eight groups, with group median speedups of 11%-224% and group maximum speedups of 11%-336%. Case studies on LiMnO2 and toluene link structure generation or spectrum elucidation, interatomic-potential relaxation, property prediction and electron-density prediction, using same-geometry density functional theory (DFT) calculations as references. For LiMnO2, predicted formation energies for generated and relaxed structures differed from same-geometry PBE+U references by at most 7 meV per atom, while the computational cost of model steps was less than one-twentieth of a DFT single-point calculation. PaddleMaterials extends unified materials workflows beyond conventional property, potential and structure-generation tasks while supporting verifiable cross-task operations and compiled execution.

papers.title: FlowBatt: Flow Matching for Probabilistic Battery Degradation Prediction
papers.abstract: Battery degradation remains a central challenge in the development and broad application of sustainable energy technologies. Accurate degradation prediction is challenging, as battery aging emerges from complex and heterogeneous interactions among cycling behavior, operating conditions, and cell chemistry. Existing machine-learning approaches typically focus on deterministic end-of-life predictions or modeling degradation curves within fixed chemistry settings, leaving probabilistic state of health (SOH) trajectory modeling across heterogeneous chemistries underexplored. We introduce FlowBatt, a use-inspired conditional generative framework that adapts flow matching with a diffusion transformer (DiT) backbone to battery degradation trajectory modeling. FlowBatt models full SOH trajectories as probabilistic degradation processes conditioned on early-cycle capacity data. To strengthen this conditioning pathway, we use explainable AI analysis to diagnose and improve the encoder that maps early-cycle capacity matrices into conditioning vectors. We evaluate FlowBatt on five public benchmark settings spanning diverse chemistries and aging conditions, comparing it with supervised and diffusion-based trajectory models as well as established baselines for remaining useful life (RUL) prediction under shared data splits. FlowBatt achieves the best trajectory-wise SOH prediction performance on all five datasets, with errors below 2.5%, and delivers competitive RUL prediction performance. By generating multiple plausible trajectories, FlowBatt provides empirical prediction intervals for battery degradation modeling. These results indicate that flow-matching-based trajectory modeling is a promising framework for probabilistic battery health prediction.

papers.title: TSB-SEG: A Systematic Time-Series Segmentation Benchmark
papers.abstract: Time-series segmentation, studied as either Change Point Detection (CPD) or State Detection (SD), underpins a broad range of monitoring and diagnostic applications. However, the field suffers from a persistent divide between the statistical community (focusing on CPD) and the machine learning and data mining communities (focusing on SD). Consequently, the literature remains fragmented: evaluations typically cover narrow methodological families, datasets are often small or homogeneous, and CPD and SD are rarely evaluated together. We address these gaps with TSB-SEG, a unified benchmark comprising 592 univariate and multivariate time series from 8 heterogeneous datasets and surveying 26 algorithms that span five decades of progress. To ensure a fair comparison, we introduce a two-pool design: a scalable main pool of tractable detectors used for the aggregate ranking, and an extended-scope pool for computationally intensive methods. All methods are unified under tsseg, an open-source library to ensure full reproducibility. Our systematic evaluation yields three insights: (a) no single detector dominates across domains, and per-dataset hyperparameter tuning remains decisive for performance, (b) CPD accuracy is a useful, though imperfect, proxy for SD accuracy, and (c) data characteristics should guide method selection. We provide actionable guidance based on data properties, error tolerances, and tuning budgets, identify impactful hyperparameters, and characterize algorithm robustness to these choices.

papers.title: Machine-learning discovery potential for a heavy Higgs boson in $e^+e^-\to ZH$ at a future lepton collider
papers.abstract: We study the discovery potential for a CP-even heavy neutral Higgs boson $H$ in the Type-I two-Higgs-doublet model (2HDM) at a future $e^+e^-$ collider with $\sqrt{s}=500~\mathrm{GeV}$, focusing on the process $e^+e^-\to ZH$ with $H\to WW$, and with $Z\to\ell\ell$ or $Z\toνν$. The final states are four jets plus two leptons ($4j2\ell$) and four jets plus missing transverse momentum ($4j2ν$). We compare a cut-based analysis with two multivariate strategies: a one-dimensional Boosted Decision Tree (BDT) trained per mass point, and a two-dimensional (BDT $\times$ $m_H$) template analysed with a profile likelihood. The 2D template improves the expected discovery significance by a factor of $2.5$--$3.6$ in the $4j2\ell$ channel and by a factor of $5$--$18$ in the $4j2ν$ channel relative to the cut-based analysis, with the largest gains at high $m_H$ where the cut-based mass window loses efficiency. We translate the expected exclusions into $95\%$ CL upper limits on $σ\times$ BR and discuss the implications for the Type-I 2HDM parameter space.

papers.title: eigenkit: A Provider-Neutral Quantum Computing Library
papers.abstract: Quantum software ecosystems provide increasingly capable tools for simulation and hardware execution, but differences in programming models, supported features, and backend capabilities can make it difficult to move and systematically compare the same quantum algorithm across execution environments. We introduce eigenkit, a provider-neutral quantum computing library that separates algorithm definition from backend execution through a common circuit representation and provider interface. The library currently supports 12 execution providers spanning simulators and quantum hardware, provides backend-independent gradient computation, and integrates with standard scientific-computing and machine-learning workflows through NumPy, PyTorch, and scikit-learn interfaces. We evaluate the practical relevance of this abstraction across both simulation and quantum hardware. Simulator performance varies substantially with circuit size, structure, batching, and application workload, showing that no single backend is consistently preferable. On quantum hardware, experiments on IBM Heron and IQM Emerald show that which processor is better suited to a given algorithm depends not only on hardware constraints, but also on how well the topology of the quantum algorithm matches the physical connectivity of the processor. These results demonstrate that backend portability is not only a software-design convenience, but can be important for both computational efficiency and quantum execution quality.

papers.title: Anion Engineering Enables Concurrent Optimization of Phonon and Carrier Transport in AMg$_2$X$_2$ Zintl Thermoelectrics
papers.abstract: The simultaneous suppression of lattice heat transport and enhancement of carrier transport is central to the development of high-performance thermoelectric materials. Here, we investigate the microscopic mechanisms governing phonon and carrier transport in CaAl$_2$Si$_2$-type AMg$_2$X$_2$ (A = Ca, Sr, Ba; X = P, As, Sb, Bi) Zintl compounds using first-principles calculations, machine-learning interatomic potentials, and Boltzmann transport theory. As X changes from P to Bi, the widening phonon band gap restricts three-phonon scattering channels and increases the relative importance of four-phonon processes. In CaMg$_2$Bi$_2$ and BaMg$_2$Bi$_2$, four-phonon scattering dominates the relaxation of low-frequency heat-carrying modes at 900 K. The Bi-based series also exhibits an anomalous increase in lattice thermal conductivity from Ca to Ba despite the increasing cation mass. Mode-resolved analysis links the lower thermal conductivity of CaMg$_2$Bi$_2$ to reduced low-frequency group velocities and stronger anharmonic scattering, with Ca-related mid-frequency vibrations providing additional four-phonon scattering channels. Including both particle-like and coherent contributions, its lattice thermal conductivity reaches 0.23 W$\cdot$m$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ at 900 K. Meanwhile, the increasing covalent character of the vertical Mg-X bonds is accompanied by enhanced band-edge dispersion and reduced carrier effective masses. These electronic changes, together with conduction-band convergence, favor n-type transport and yield a predicted peak $ZT$ of 3.68 at 900 K in CaMg$_2$Bi$_2$. These results elucidate the interplay of phonon spectral structure and higher-order anharmonicity in thermal transport, alongside the distinct electronic response to anion substitution.

papers.title: Multipartite FSO/QKD with N-GHZ States for Scalable Secure Group Key Distribution
papers.abstract: The emergence of sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks is driving the need for secure group key generation mechanisms resilient to quantum-computing attacks. Conventional quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols are designed for point-to-point communication and are therefore not directly applicable to group key establishment. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a scalable High-Altitude Platform (HAP)-assisted multipartite QKD network architecture that integrates $N$-GHZ-state protocols with a Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) scheme over free-space optical (FSO) channels. The performance of the proposed system is evaluated using a Qiskit-based simulation framework that incorporates realistic physical-layer impairments of FSO links. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed architecture significantly improves the group secret key rate (SKR) compared to conventional bipartite approaches, while effectively reducing overall network execution delay. In addition, the analysis reveals the impact of channel impairments and provides practical design insights, such as optimal beam-waist control. The proposed framework demonstrates the potential of HAP-assisted multipartite QKD as an effective security solution for future large-scale 6G wireless networks supporting secure group communications.

papers.title: Structure of energy flux densities in Earth's magnetotail reconnection regions: Bridging simulation and observation
papers.abstract: Magnetic reconnection is important in both space and laboratory contexts because it changes the topology of magnetic fields and converts magnetic energy into particle energies. Establishing where this energy conversion occurs is critical for understanding how reconnection partitions energy. Using a novel machine learning approach based on simulations that explicitly identifies the separatrix regions for the first time, the partition of energy flux densities within the magnetic reconnection site is evaluated through statistical study of magnetotail reconnection events observed in situ. The separatrices are found to have the largest electron energy flux densities, roughly twice those in the exhaust, and Poynting flux densities about four times those in the inflows, whereas typical ion enthalpy flux densities are largest in the exhaust. The separatrices are therefore sites of intense electron and electromagnetic energy transport, although their small thickness means that the exhaust may still carry most of the total energy flux.

papers.title: Reimagining computational quantum research with AI scientists
papers.abstract: AI scientists are expanding automated research across scientific domains, yet their ability to turn the scientific record into a foundation for autonomous discovery remains elusive. Here we uncover a fundamental barrier to this transition and demonstrate a route to overcome it in computational quantum science, where advances shape both what we can learn from complex quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. To identify this barrier, we introduce OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment that converts published studies into executable reproduction tasks. Across 59 papers spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization, we systematically evaluate five agentic systems powered by large language models and six third-party agent harnesses. Our findings reveal that current AI scientists often fail to reproduce published results, exposing a fundamental mismatch between what scientific papers communicate and what autonomous agents require. By contrast, human expert intervention can turn these failures into successful reproductions, showing that the missing information can be identified and converted into reusable research experience. Guided by this observation, we develop Residual Agents (RA), a quantum-tailored self-improving AI scientist that distils externally verified workflow repairs into such experience. RA substantially improves research performance under fixed base models and limited adaptation budgets. For example, RA raises DeepSeek V4.1 Flash performance from 68% to 85%, matching Claude Code with Opus 5 at a third of its cost despite using a weaker base model. We integrate all reproduced results into an extensible platform built on the model context protocol, making verified research workflows directly accessible to AI scientists and allowing new scientific papers to be continuously incorporated.

papers.title: RxnMiner: A Multimodal Agent for Structured Reaction Data Extraction from Chemistry Figures
papers.abstract: Reaction data underpin machine learning for reaction prediction, condition recommendation, and retrosynthetic planning, yet extracting these data from literature figures still requires substantial manual effort. Many figures encode multiple experiments through shared templates, substituent tables, and product grids. Recovering concrete reaction records therefore requires molecular recognition, association of evidence with individual experimental entries, and reconstruction of indirectly specified participants. We present RxnMiner, a multimodal agent system that combines an expert-informed extraction procedure with a chemistry toolbox to coordinate these operations. The agent reads molecular structures, resolves shared and entry-specific evidence, and instantiates participants from templates to assemble source-linked reaction records. We also introduce ChemRxn-Bench, a benchmark of 603 reaction figures with 8,547 manually annotated and reviewed reaction records, evaluated under a common protocol for exact molecular identity and reactant-product pairing. On this benchmark, with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as the backbone, RxnMiner raises stereochemistry-aware reaction macro-F1 from 21.0% under direct prediction to 71.0%, compared with 25.0% for the strongest existing extraction system. Across five backbones, it also outperforms the same base agent without the extraction procedure and chemistry toolbox by 9.4 to 25.5 points. Applied without human intervention to 10,107 literature figures, RxnMiner produces a silver corpus of 88,202 source-linked reaction records.

papers.title: Local Zero-Shot Latency Prediction for Low-End GPUs
papers.abstract: Quantifying execution latency is an important consideration across Machine Learning. Existing latency-prediction approaches typically train ML models on traces collected from workload execution on target hardware. Collection of representative traces across many consumer GPUs is expensive both in organizing the devices and in manpower, causing existing work to mainly focus on a limited set of high-end GPUs available in cloud computing. To offset this cost, we show that a local host GPU can be configured to reproduce the execution performance of less powerful target GPUs. Through selectively modifying device parameters, we obtain locally measured latencies that closely approximate those observed on the target hardware. We reformulate the latency-prediction task: instead of fitting a prediction model to a dataset of execution traces, we identify local configurations that best reproduce target devices' performance, enabling zero-shot prediction. We evaluate our approach against real measurements from 60 computer-vision models executed on 21 consumer GPU models. Our method achieves a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 14.21%, compared with more than 25% for comparable baselines, reducing relative prediction error by 43.6%. Predicted and measured latencies exhibit an average Spearman correlation of 0.961 across training tasks, demonstrating that the method also accurately preserves performance rankings across devices.

papers.title: Two Fast Radio Burst Candidates Detected in the RATAN-600 Blind Survey
papers.abstract: We report the detection of two single dispersed pulses with widths of about 6.7\,ms and 15.6\,ms and flux densities of about 0.8 and 1.7\,Jy. These were found in a blind survey of two circular regions (Dec$\;=+22^{\circ}$ and $+5^{\circ}$,RA: 0--24~h) at high radio frequencies \mbox{(4400--5000\,MHz)} using four 4-channel filter radiometers (central frequencies of 4475, 4625, 4775, and 4925\,MHz)   spanning a total frequency bandwidth of 600\,MHz. The survey was carried out with the Western Sector antenna of the RATAN-600 radio telescope, which had an effective area of 1200\,m$^2$ in~2017--2025. The total area of the survey was about 1500~square degrees, and each pointing of the antenna lasted one year. We consider these to be two rare, high-frequency FRB events (MJD~58614.38257 and MJD~58659.62482), detected with estimated dispersion measures of $200\pm20$ and $266\pm10$\,pc\,cm$^{-3}$ at a final signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) level of 8--9 after additional optimal filtration. After subtraction of the estimated dispersions within the Milky Way, we estimated redshifts of approximately 0.09 and 0.13, respectively, using the traditional equation: ${\rm DM}\,[{\rm pc~cm}^{-3}] = 1000\,z$ for the intergalactic medium. The estimated isotropic energies of the FRBs are equal to $10^{40}$\,erg and $2\times 10^{40}$\,erg, respectively. To effectively detect single pulses, we applied machine learning methods using a neural network trained on synthetic FRB pulse profiles.

papers.title: Constructing an Artworld Influencers Network by Mining Social Media
papers.abstract: The author shows a methodology for constructing a network map of the artworld. The tweets posted by a manually comprised set of exemplar artworld actors and Natural Language Processing (NLP) methods are used to identify significant artworld actors, including those that do not own a Twitter account. Identified artworld actors form communities detected with the Louvain method, and their authority is evaluated with the HITS centrality method. The resulting artworld network exhibits the ability, starting with a small set of exemplar actors, to identify new artworld actors and provides a wealth of data that would be very hard to collect otherwise.

papers.title: Variable names provide priors: semantic grounding enables data-efficient numerical prediction by large language models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across diverse tasks, from question answering to code generation. Recent studies have found that LLMs can perform numerical prediction on tabular datasets via in-context learning. However, it remains unclear under what conditions and how LLMs use variable names and in-context examples for numerical prediction. Here we show that semantic grounding, the match between variable names and the values they describe, allows five LLMs without task-specific training to match or outperform seven supervised machine learning (ML) models across 20 datasets from nine scientific domains, particularly when examples are scarce. Reasoning traces indicate that variable names allow LLMs to draw on domain-specific knowledge acquired during pretraining. Using controlled tasks based on physical formulas, we further show that LLMs integrate domain-specific knowledge with in-context examples in a way consistent with Bayesian updating. Specifically, when the relationship between the inputs and the target cannot be inferred from the examples alone, LLMs rely on domain-specific knowledge as the prior. Conversely, as contradicting examples accumulate, LLM predictions shift progressively towards these examples, which act as the likelihood. Our work reveals how LLMs use domain-specific knowledge in numerical prediction and positions them as data-efficient predictors for data-scarce scientific domains.

papers.title: Evolving Explanations: Complexity-Adaptive Refinement of Faithful Explanations for Symbolic Regression
papers.abstract: Natural-language explanations generated by large language models (LLMs) for machine learning models often seem fluent but are not necessarily faithful to the underlying model. We formalize this mismatch as a faithfulness gap and propose a complexity-adaptive refinement framework for symbolic regression that iteratively generates and validates explanations until numerical agreement with the target expression is achieved. The approach follows a two-stage pipeline: an explainer LLM produces textual descriptions at increasing levels of detail, while an independent validator LLM extracts a symbolic expression that is compared against the original model. This process is framed as a discrete search over explanation space, where complexity is minimized subject to a faithfulness constraint. We evaluate the method on real-world and synthetic datasets, with a total of 250 runs across varying model complexities. The explanation refinement loop achieves an overall pass rate of 84.0%, with most explanations converging at low complexity levels and only a small fraction requiring detailed descriptions. Our results demonstrate that faithful explanations can be obtained with minimal necessary complexity by explicitly closing the explanation loop through symbolic validation.

papers.title: Collective dipole effects amplify field-driven ion transport in amorphous Li$_3$PO$_4$
papers.abstract: Amorphous solid electrolytes often outperform their crystalline counterparts, but how disorder shapes ionic transport under strong electric fields is poorly understood. We use molecular dynamics with a machine-learned interatomic potential and a machine-learned Born-effective-charge model to measure Li mobility in amorphous Li$_3$PO$_4$ and in a crystal with Li vacancies, from the linear to the strongly nonlinear regime. The amorphous phase shows a much stronger field enhancement, and we trace this to a collective dipole effect. The migrating ion carries the same charge in both phases. Alone it would not make the amorphous phase respond more strongly. What makes the difference is the environment. In the amorphous network the surrounding atoms move with the hop. Their motion makes the work the field performs vary widely between hops. Since hopping rates grow exponentially with the work, the most strongly assisted hops can dominate the drift. Disorder thus enhances field-driven transport through the environment rather than the carrier itself, a mechanism that may operate in disordered ion conductors in general.

papers.title: Enhancing Stock Market Information Retrieval with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has been widely applied in financial domains, enabling automated analysis and retrieval of stock market information. However, traditional NLP-based systems often struggle with maintaining contextual accuracy and generating relevant responses in dynamic financial environments. To address these challenges, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have emerged as a powerful solution, combining retrieval-based methods with generative capabilities to enhance response quality. In this study, we present a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed to generate responses related to stock market information. The system integrates retrieval-based and generative approaches to enhance the accuracy and relevance of financial text generation. To evaluate its effectiveness, we employ the ROUGE metric, specifically ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L, to measure lexical and structural similarity between generated and reference texts. Experimental results on a dataset of 100 stock market-related queries demonstrate high ROUGE scores, indicating strong alignment with reference documents. Additionally, we assess latency to evaluate the system responsiveness, achieving an average response time of 1.16 seconds. These findings confirm that our RAG model is capable of providing accurate and timely stock market insights, making it a promising approach for financial information retrieval.

papers.title: Learning the Entropic Relaxation: Stable Coarse-Grid Emulation with Neural Discrete Equilibrium
papers.abstract: The ability to emulate complicated and computationally-expensive physical systems in an efficient and stable manner is a popular motivation for scientific machine learning (SciML). Stable numerical solvers tend to be computationally expensive, as they attempt to resolve small (spatial and temporal) scales that receive and dissipate spectral energy. Learned coarse-grid forecasters remove the dissipative channel, allowing unresolved frequencies to re-emerge as grid-scale noise (aliasing). In this paper, we use the Neural Discrete Equilibrium (NeurDE) method to explore stable emulation at extremely coarse grids, demonstrating physically-principled control over entropy dynamics that reinforces the physical system's dissipative mechanism. Entropically-stabilized NeurDE produces stable long-time rollouts for thousands of forecasting steps on large Reynolds number turbulent flows ($\mathrm{Re}=100{,}000$) with very coarse grids (down to $\mathbb{R}^{16\times16}$). At these very coarse grid scales, entropically-stabilized NeurDE can be more stable than even our stabilized data-generation numerical method.

papers.title: Architecture-Aware Mixed Precision for Replica-Exchange Training of Geometry-Aware Neural Operators with Uncertainty Quantification
papers.abstract: Geometry-aware neural operators face substantial computational and memory demands when learning across complex physical domains. We introduce Architecture-Aware Mixed Precision (AA-MP), a replica-exchange training strategy that allocates numerical precision according to replica roles and architecture-specific operations. By retaining FP32 for refinement while selectively employing BF16 for exploration, AA-MP preserves predictive accuracy while improving training efficiency. Across fluid dynamics and three-dimensional structural mechanics benchmarks, AA-MP achieves comparable accuracy to full-precision training over an ensemble of runs, while reducing hot-replica peak GPU memory by 46.9% and training time by up to 25.8%. It also outperforms naive Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) in memory efficiency and computational cost, with increasing memory advantages at larger model and geometry scales. Ablation studies show that retaining FP32 in the cold-replica is important for predictive accuracy, while additional FP32 operations in the exploratory replica provide limited benefits relative to their computational cost. Finally, conformal prediction for uncertainty calibration shows that AA-MP achieves near-nominal coverage with narrower prediction intervals than the alternatives. These results advance the scalability of geometry-aware scientific machine learning by reducing computational costs without compromising predictive accuracy or uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: A Novel Federated Learning Framework for Defending Against Gradient Inversion Attacks
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) offers a paradigm for collaborative machine learning model training among clients, preserving data privacy by avoiding direct data sharing. However, the gradient information exchanged in FL has been shown to be vulnerable to Gradient Inversion Attacks (GIA), which can reconstruct sensitive user data. To counter these threats, various privacy-enhancing technologies like Secure Multi-party Computing (SMC), Homomorphic Encryption (HE), and Differential Privacy (DP) have been integrated into FL. While effective, these methods often introduce significant trade-offs between privacy and model utility. By revisiting the key to privacy exposure in FL under GIA, which lies in the frequent sharing of model gradients that contain private data, we take a new perspective by designing a novel privacy-preserving FL framework that effectively ``breaks the direct connection'' between the shared parameters and the local private data to defend against GIA. Our proposed framework, HyperFL++, leverages hypernetworks to generate local model parameters, where only the hypernetwork parameters are aggregated by the server. To ensure practicality, HyperFL++ incorporates a Row-wise Kronecker Decomposition (RKD) to mitigate the memory and communication overhead from the hypernetwork. Comprehensive theoretical analysis and extensive experiments validate our method's effectiveness in protecting data privacy while maintaining high model utility. Our code is available at https://github.com/Pengxin-Guo/HyperFL/tree/hyperfl%2B%2B.

papers.title: Machine-Learned Interatomic Potential for the Mo-S-Al-O System
papers.abstract: We develop a machine-learned neuroevolution potential (NEP) for the Mo-S-Al-O system, targeting MoS$_2$ heteroepitaxy on c-plane sapphire, $α$-Al$_2$O$_3$(0001). The potential is trained on 63,611 PBE+D3 structures distilled from about 1.1 million curated density-functional-theory (DFT) configurations, using an energy-difference loss function that directly targets interfacial and orientation-dependent energies. On held-out data, the energy and force errors are 29 meV/atom and 0.23 eV/$\mathring{A}$. Validated against DFT on a suite of physical properties, the NEP reproduces the lattice constants within 0.3 %, the elastic constants within 17 %, the phonon dispersions with mean deviations below 2.5%, and the surface energies within 1.3 %. At the MoS$_2$/sapphire interface, it reproduces the adhesion energy minimum within 0.8 %, the interfacial energy within 2.2 % and the most stable orientation of the monolayer. It preserves the DFT-predicted energetic ordering of edges, point defects (Spearman $ρ$ = 0.995) and mirror-twin boundaries ($ρ$ = 1.0), and reproduces tilt grain-boundary energies within 8 % ($ρ$ = 0.98) and stacking-fault energy barriers within 14 %. The resulting potential enables future studies of the atomic-scale mechanisms of defect formation in two-dimensional heteroepitaxy.

papers.title: GPU infrastructure for ML/MM with electrostatic embedding for enzyme chemistry
papers.abstract: We present a fully GPU-native framework for machine learning/molecular mechanics (ML/MM) enhanced sampling simulations with electrostatic embedding, demonstrated on an enzymatic reaction. The framework combines a JAX port of the pretrained MACE-POLAR-1-M model, an electrostatic embedding scheme compatible with the MACE-POLAR architecture, and integration with JAX-MD and PLUMED-JAX for end-to-end compiled enhanced sampling. The implementation is developed using GPT-6.1-Sol within Codex, with reasoning effort set to high. Using replica exchange umbrella sampling, we calculate the free energy profile of nucleophilic substitution in haloalkane dehalogenase in approximately 200 H100 GPU hours, treating the entire protein and reactants with MACE-POLAR-1-M-JAX and most of the solvent with molecular mechanics.

papers.title: Improving Financial Cybersecurity Through Fraud Transaction Detection with Deep Learning
papers.abstract: Financial fraud detection remains a critical challenge in cybersecurity, with traditional rule-based systems struggling to keep pace with evolving attack patterns. This paper presents a deep learning approach for fraud transaction detection, leveraging neural network architectures to identify anomalous financial behaviors with high accuracy. We evaluate multiple deep learning models including LSTM, CNN, and hybrid architectures on real-world financial transaction datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over conventional machine learning baselines. Our approach achieves robust performance in detecting fraudulent transactions while minimizing false positives, providing a scalable solution for enterprise financial cybersecurity systems

papers.title: Metamorphic Testing for Evaluating Robustness of Sentiment Analysis Models
papers.abstract: Machine learning systems are challenging to test using traditional software testing methods because their behavior is learned from data rather than explicitly programmed. This challenge is particularly significant in natural language processing (NLP), where small input variations can lead to unexpected model behavior. Conventional evaluation metrics, such as accuracy and F1-score, often fail to capture such inconsistencies. Metamorphic testing addresses this limitation by evaluating expected relationships between original and transformed inputs. With the increasing prevalence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and language-based AI systems, the need for systematic robustness testing has become even more pronounced. Motivated by this growing need, this paper presents a lightweight, batch-based metamorphic testing approach for evaluating the robustness of such systems. In particular, we consider sentiment analysis as a representative NLP task and evaluate a pretrained classifier under four transformations: synonym replacement, typo injection, word-order variation, and negation. Using consistency score, flip accuracy, and confidence change, we identify strengths in handling semantic variations and vulnerabilities to textual noise and logical transformations. These findings highlight the value of metamorphic testing in identifying behavioral inconsistencies beyond conventional performance metrics and demonstrate its potential as a systematic framework for evaluating the robustness of language-based AI systems and guiding performance improvements before deployment.

papers.title: Fuzzy-Enhanced Machine Learning Approach for Type 2 Diabetes Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Accurate diabetes prediction is critical for early clinical intervention, yet existing machine-learning pipelines often fail due to class imbalance, noisy physiological measurements, and redundant or weakly informative features. To address these unresolved limitations, this study establishes a unified fuzzy-evolutionary-ensemble framework designed to uncover a more discriminative feature space for type 2 diabetes prediction. The workflow integrates selective fuzzification of nonlinear clinical variables, SMOTE-ENN-based balancing and noise filtering, and Bat-Algorithm-driven evolutionary feature selection prior to training a Random Forest classifier. Applied to the Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset, the framework compresses the expanded fuzzy-numerical space into an optimized 10-feature subset and yields substantial performance gains: 96.11% accuracy, 95.14% precision, 98.00% recall, and a 98.23% F1-score. Relative to a baseline Random Forest using all 16 features (74.45% accuracy; 59.86% F1), the system achieves more than a 1.6-fold improvement in F1-score while preserving over 99% stability in majority-class detection and surpassing earlier published 16-feature models impacted by imbalance and weak feature relevance. Collectively, these results demonstrate that the integrated pipeline produces an enhanced fuzzy-numerical representation space that improves diabetes risk stratification and provides a scalable, uncertainty-aware foundation for diagnostic modeling across broader clinical datasets.

papers.title: Extrapolation and explainability in hadron mass predictions with machine learning
papers.abstract: In this work, we study the predictive performance of four machine learning (ML) models for hadron masses, with particular attention to extrapolation beyond the conventional hadrons represented in the training data. Calculations are performed using a multilayer perceptron (MLP), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Gaussian process regression (GPR). ML models are trained on conventional hadrons, using features that describe valence quark content and quantum numbers. Then, we evaluate their performance on test sets and on a separate extrapolation set of 39 states, including exotic candidates and heavy baryons, none of which appear in the training or test sets. We find that the MLP achieves the lowest extrapolation Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) on the $30$ states with measured masses at $294.2 \pm 57.9$~MeV, roughly one-third that of the other models. We also show that the MLP reproduces the overall mass scale of nine unobserved doubly heavy baryons predicted by theoretical calculations, although it underestimates the doubly bottom masses. We use SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis and show that heavy quark content is the most significant factor in the MLP's mass predictions, with the remaining features contributing differently across hadron types. Our results quantify the extrapolation accuracy of ML models for hadron masses and identify the features that drive the MLP predictions.

papers.title: A Matched Evaluation of QUBO Action Models and Defensive Remediation in Cyber Attack Graphs
papers.abstract: This study examines how vulnerability-specific actions affect quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) models for minimum-cost cyber attack paths and defensive remediation. Edge-flow and variable-length hop formulations are evaluated using simulated annealing, steepest descent, and tabu search against exact classical references. Experiments on six independent synthetic topologies separate the effects of transition eligibility, vulnerability labels, exploit costs, and multiple exploit alternatives. A single labeled action per eligible transition preserves feasible paths, optimal costs, and QUBO size. Under the tested settings, multiple exploit alternatives were associated with approximately unchanged valid-path recovery, lower optimal-path recovery, and substantially larger representations, particularly for the hop formulation. These recovery differences remain descriptive because they are not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. An evaluation on a published 3CX attack graph with synthetic costs demonstrates applicability beyond the generated topologies. The defensive extension selects patches within a budget to raise attack-path costs to specified thresholds or disconnect protected targets. Against exhaustive and mixed-integer references, the tested QUBO heuristics recovered an optimal patch set in 12 of 16 calls across eight scenarios on one topology.   The results characterize formulation correctness, solution recovery, and resource requirements using classical local optimization, without establishing quantum computational advantage.

papers.title: Black-Box Adversarial Example Attacks on Machine Learning based Election Systems
papers.abstract: Machine learning models have shown exceptional accuracy for ballot classification in election systems. Recent research has demonstrated that these ballot classification models are vulnerable to adversarial example attacks. This is a critical security issue because a successful attack could alter the outcome of an election and undermine the democratic process. However, all adversarial example attacks in the voting domain have assumed a white-box threat model, where the classifier parameters are known. In this work, we advance the field of machine learning in election systems by analyzing a realistic black-box adversary. We implement and evaluate eleven state-of-the-art black-box attacks: query based attacks ADBA, Square, SurFree, RayS, and SA-MOO. We also test adaptive transfer based black-box attacks with APGD-$l_\infty$, APGD-$l_2$, APGD-$l_1$, PGD $l_0$, PGD $l_0$+$l_\infty$, and PGD $l_0$+$σ$. Our attacks span multiple different norms ($l_\infty$, $l_2$, $l_1$, and $l_0$) and three different black-box adversarial threat models (decision based, score based and transfer based). In addition to digital analyses, we physically print and scan $20,000$ adversarial examples to evaluate the real-world performance of different black-box attacks. Our finding demonstrate an even larger physical-digital robustness gap exists for black-box adversarial examples than for white-box adversarial examples. Lastly, we conduct the first ever adversarial example transferability study in the voting domain and test adversarial training and barrier zones as two possible black-box defense strategies.

papers.title: ZT-DAC: ML-Driven Dynamic Access Control Policy for Zero Trust in DER Networks
papers.abstract: The increasing penetration of Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) in the smart grid has significantly expanded the cyber-attack surface. Traditionally, DER networks rely on static role-based access control (RBAC) mechanisms that assume persistent trust after authentication. This limitation enables adversaries to maintain unauthorized privileges and move laterally across DER systems, disrupting grid operations. Although attribute-based access control (ABAC) enables fine-grained and context-aware access decisions, it does not fully eliminate implicit trust. Zero Trust (ZT) principles can be incorporated to enhance ABAC policies. This paper proposes a dynamic access control framework for implementing ZT in DER networks (ZT-DAC). The proposed solution employs a two-stage verification process and integrates an Open Policy Agent (OPA)-based RBAC with a machine learning (ML)-based ABAC to enforce continuous and adaptive trust score assessment. To support realistic DER operations, a DER-specific access control model is developed and used to generate a domain-informed dataset of access requests incorporating both legitimate and adversarial behaviors. Experimental results on the dataset show that the OPA-based decision layer achieves \(91.92\%\) accuracy, with a False Positive Rate of \(14.45\%\), while the ML model achieves a Mean Absolute Error of \(2.074\) and an \(R^2\) of \(0.891\) in trust-score prediction. The ABAC layer achieves \(93.27\%\) accuracy, with a FPR of \(3.88\%\), validating its practical feasibility within realistic DER environments.

papers.title: Reduced Cost Influence Functions for Predict-then-Optimize under Noisy Data
papers.abstract: Machine learning models deployed in decision-making pipelines, from vehicle routing to dynamic pricing to clinical decision support, must remain reliable in the face of low-quality training data. We study a predict-then-optimize setting in which an upstream model predicts the cost vector of a downstream linear program, with a large pool of noisy training data supplemented by a small curated set of clean data. We introduce Reduced Cost Influence Functions (RCIFs), which combine influence functions from robust statistics with the geometry of linear optimization to estimate how each training point shifts downstream decisions. Building on this, we propose a reweighting algorithm that uses RCIFs to downweight harmful training points and reduce downstream regret. Experiments on random linear programs and shortest-path problems show that our approach reduces regret, and accompanying theory characterizes properties of RCIFs and identifies regimes favorable to our method relative to baselines.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning in High-Energy Physics: A Survey from Accelerator Control to Theory Exploration
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a machine learning paradigm in which an agent learns a decision-making policy by interacting with an environment, guided by a scalar reward rather than explicit supervision. Supervised and unsupervised learning have become indispensable tools in high-energy physics (HEP), but they learn from fixed datasets, whereas many HEP tasks are closed-loop decisions: the data an algorithm observes depend on its choices, the feedback is sparse or delayed, and the objective is often measured on a real machine or in a stochastic simulation, not by a differentiable model. This survey reviews the application of RL to such tasks: accelerator control and feedback, data quality monitoring, jet grooming, clustering, and representation, charged particle tracking, beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) and string model building, detector design, trigger control, analysis, and formal quantum field theory computation. It provides a self-contained introduction to the underlying RL methods, from model-free and model-based to multi-agent, offline, inverse, and bandit approaches, reviews each domain against its traditional methods, and summarizes the head-to-head comparisons. The applications range from policies deployed on real accelerators and evaluated on recorded collision data to exploratory studies in formal theory. RL is most advantageous for repeated tasks with a fast simulator, decisions inside fast control loops, operation under faults and corrupted measurements, physics-based rewards in place of labels, and sequential discrete constructions with a reusable policy, while Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, and differentiable methods remain competitive elsewhere. We conclude with the open challenges that recur across domains, including reward design, sim-to-real transfer, safety, the lack of shared benchmarks, and the statistical validity of policy-driven decisions.

papers.title: QueueTrack: Framework for Detecting the Onset of Queueing in Mobile Networks
papers.abstract: In mobile networks, timely and accurate detection of the onset of queueing at path bottlenecks remains challenging for end-to-end congestion control algorithms (CCAs), where end hosts have limited visibility into queue status. Traditional congestion signals, such as packet loss, round-trip time (RTT), and one-way delay (OWD), have well-known limitations for early queue buildup detection. This paper presents QueueTrack, a practical end-host framework to detect the onset of queueing in mobile networks. QueueTrack computes a queue buildup indicator, denoted QBI, from endpoint-observable packet-level timing statistics, without requiring tight synchronization between end hosts or modifications to the existing network infrastructure. We develop and assess the complete QueueTrack machine learning (ML) pipeline, including data collection, labeling, model training, and testing, on a 5G testbed built on the OpenAirInterface platform, under a range of scenarios with competing TCP traffic. The experimental results show that QueueTrack can reliably detect the onset of queueing at the 5G base station using low-complexity classification models such as logistic regression. For example, QueueTrack achieves an F1 score of approximately 80% in a challenging mixed TCP/UDP scenario. These findings confirm that QueueTrack can serve as a practical framework for developing CCAs that target low delay, as well as for network telemetry and network monitoring in mobile networks.

papers.title: Rule-based hardware-configurable static analysis for quantum programs
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of quantum hardware necessitates an adaptable static analysis framework for validating quantum programs. In this work, we introduce SHARP, a rule-based static analysis framework designed for OpenQASM that decouples hardware-specific constraints from the validation engine. By employing a rule-based approach, SHARP allows quantum computing services to validate programs against evolving instruction set architectures (ISAs) without having to modify the core analysis engine. SHARP achieves this by ingesting ISA descriptions as standalone data, making the validation engine resilient to hardware updates. Furthermore, the framework employs an analysis-driven validation mechanism that enables multi-stage validation, simplifying rule construction and enhancing extensibility. We demonstrate how SHARP supports hardware-specific validation tasks and discuss its impact on quantum software development, including language decoupling, program-level constraint validation, and feature access control. Our findings suggest that SHARP provides a path toward a scalable and maintainable programming interface for quantum computing.

papers.title: Quantum Path Finder: Navigating Constraint Space via Non-Abelian Gauge Dynamics
papers.abstract: Quantum algorithms are commonly designed within the circuit paradigm or through adiabatic evolution. Here we introduce \emph{Quantum Path Finder} (QPF), a distinct algorithm-design paradigm based on non-Abelian gauge dynamics in a constraint-protected degenerate manifold. Each Boolean variable is promoted to a qutrit whose additional state represents an unassigned variable. The problem Hamiltonian then defines a connected manifold of feasible partial assignments, and time-dependent local qutrit rotations generate coherent transport on this manifold. Unlike conventional adiabatic quantum computation, QPF does not require the state to follow an instantaneous eigenstate along a prescribed interpolation: adiabaticity with respect to the constraint gap protects the feasible manifold, while adiabatic following within that manifold is optional. The algorithmic task is therefore to design paths and interference in constraint space rather than only to engineer a sequence of gates or a ground-state interpolation. We illustrate the framework with three applications. For unstructured search, a two-level analysis and numerical evolution recover Grover-type scaling under explicitly stated assumptions. For complete $3$-XORSAT, the accessible gauge sector has a size-independent gap, in contrast to the exponentially closing gap of a conventional transverse-field adiabatic path. For satisfiable $3$-SAT instances, finite-size benchmarks demonstrate high satisfied-clause fractions at short classical comparison budgets, without claiming an equal-cost quantum advantage. We also outline a superconducting-qutrit implementation and discuss the conceptual relationship between QPF and nondeterministic Turing machine.

papers.title: Exact factorization of finite-range three-body matrix elements between Gaussian wave packets and its application to the $0^+$ states of $^{12}C$
papers.abstract: We introduce finite-range three-body interactions into the $β-γ$-constrained generator coordinate method of antisymmetrized molecular dynamics. These genuine operators give saturation without an additional prescription for the projection, but require $O(A^6)$ complex exponentials at every node of the projection grid. With the graph Laplacian of the ranges, as in spectral clustering widely used in machine learning, we factorize the exponential factor of a Gaussian three-body kernel exactly into pairwise tables of $O(A^2)$ exponentials. A cofactor expansion rewrites the remaining contraction as complex matrix-matrix products. For $^{12}C$, the factorization reduces the time of the kernels with the three-body term from $530$ to $24$ times that of the two-body kernels. We apply the method to the $0^+$ states of $^{12}C$ with the Volkov, Tohsaki F1, and Kanada-En'yo--Akaishi F3B interactions, restricting the intrinsic states to time-reversal-invariant ones. Without the three-body terms of F1 and F3B, $^{12}C$ collapses far below the three $α$ threshold, whereas with them the ground state lies close to its experimental position below the threshold. When we adjust the Majorana parameter to this position, the Hoyle state lies within 0.6 MeV of experiment for all three interactions.

papers.title: Machine Learning Beyond Statistical Consistency for Hybrid AI
papers.abstract: We propose a new definition of machine learning, according to which a machine learns a function when it computes the function successfully, that is, when the value it returns for each input has a proper derivation in a formal system. We extend Gödel's Representability Theorem, which equates computation with derivation, to empirical targets in two ways: the theorem is extended to the computable reals, and the data are admitted into the system as empirical definitions that record what has been observed. We prove that a machine learns a true probability if and only if two conditions are met. The Truth Condition is that its estimate converges to the true probability, which is statistical consistency. The Assurance Condition is that the machine properly derives its own convergence inside the system. Learning thus lies beyond statistical consistency, for it requires a derivation of the convergence from the record. A global assumption about the data, such as the i.i.d. assumption, does not supply such a derivation, because it leads only to a circular one, as we show for PAC learning. On the other hand, the two conditions are met for the probability of a sentence over a finite ideal corpus. A real machine can approximate a true probability only if an ideal machine can learn it precisely, that is, only in a domain that meets the two conditions. Modern AI works in such a domain, and we offer this as a clue to its success. Modern AI is hybrid as well, in two senses: First, it performs two kinds of tasks, namely probabilistic ones such as predicting the next word and deductive ones such as proving and coding. Second, it combines two parts of different kinds, a statistical proposer and a deductive verifier, for proving and coding. Our framework explains both senses of hybridity in one formal system.

papers.title: Robust Remote ECG Monitoring under Energy Constraints: Anomaly Filtering versus Predictive Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Machine learning for remote electrocardiogram monitoring must handle noise and diseases absent from training under tight resource constraints. We investigate whether upstream unsupervised anomaly detection can improve monitoring decisions more efficiently than classifier-derived uncertainty. We evaluate five detectors on PTB-XL and BUT QDB and compare a two-stage filter-classifier system with Monte Carlo Dropout and deep ensembles under unseen-disease and noise conditions. Performance is averaged over five training seeds. We measure single-pass energy, latency, and graph memory on a microcontroller's central processing unit (CPU) and neural processing unit (NPU). Per-score neural network costs account for repeated evaluations but exclude scoring outside deployed graphs. Energy equations relate filtering and rejection to avoided classifier execution. Across four disease scenarios, Deep Support Vector Data Description (Deep SVDD) achieves the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve within all tested finite CPU energy budgets. On the NPU, it leads at 1 mJ, while Monte Carlo Dropout has slightly higher means at 10 and 100 mJ. With a narrow CPU classifier, the Deep SVDD two-stage system increases the fraction of correctly classified or correctly rejected inputs by 15.0-19.4 percentage points over classification without rejection. Estimated energy per input is 1.93-6.99 mJ, compared with 52.53 mJ for Monte Carlo Dropout and 8.76-17.51 mJ for deep ensembles, at each method's retrospectively selected test accuracy peak. These results support upstream filtering for efficient remote monitoring, while independent validation and complete-system measurements remain necessary.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Agentic Workflows via Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks
papers.abstract: Agentic workflows organize complex tasks into reusable procedures. However, invoking an LLM at every step incurs repeated inference costs and delays. We propose a framework for self-evolving agentic workflows through semantic task decomposition. Each subtask has explicit applicability conditions and a procedure that executes code or invokes a model as needed. An agent uses execution feedback to refine the decomposition and update these procedures. Experiments in the GLEE competition show the framework on bargaining, negotiation and persuasion. Most observed final-decision procedures are implemented in code. Code is available at https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/NeurIPS2026_SeaFlow.

papers.title: Comparative Strategies for Handling Imbalanced QSAR Regression: A Case Study on hERG Activity Prediction
papers.abstract: Data imbalance frequently occurs in QSAR modeling, yet most studies focus on classification tasks, and few address regression tasks, as it is challenging to determine which regions of the data are sparse or dense. Data-level and algorithm-level imbalance-handling strategies can have different effects on model performance. In this study, we systematically compare various strategies across GCN and fingerprint-based machine learning models. To evaluate model performance more meaningfully, we partitioned the target region into several subregions based on both domain knowledge and data distribution. We focused on the region of greatest practical interest. Our results demonstrate that selecting models based on this interest-region metric leads to more reliable performance than using the total region metric. We also observed that different imbalance-handling strategies can have divergent effects depending on the model type. These findings highlight the importance of region-aware evaluation in regression QSAR modeling and provide practical guidance for selecting appropriate strategies for imbalanced datasets.

papers.title: Sonny-ENS: demystifying machine-learning ensemble weather forecasting
papers.abstract: Every weather forecast is uncertain, and decisions from flood warnings to energy trading depend on how well that uncertainty is quantified. Machine-learning (ML) ensembles now quantify it better than the best physics-based ensemble, yet two things about them remain opaque: whether their skill requires hundreds to thousands of accelerator-days of training, and how a network with a simple source of randomness produces a spread that follows the flow. Here we introduce Sonny-ENS, an ensemble of three 68.9-million-parameter networks with Monte Carlo dropout, trained on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) in 2.7 A40 GPU-days. On 2022, it has a lower CRPS than the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble (ENS) on 96% of 570 targets and an 8.3% lower mean CRPS at lead times of 1-10 days. It outperforms the operational GenCast on 69% of the targets, and a 51-member, 15-day forecast takes 69 s on one GPU. Ablations identify the ingredients of this skill, and a Kolmogorov-Arnold sparse autoencoder shows that dropout injects uncertainty mainly in the tropics, whereas the spread grows where the atmosphere is baroclinically unstable (spatial correlation 0.91 with the Eady growth rate). Skillful probabilistic weather forecasts are therefore within reach of a single GPU server.

papers.title: InformedXRD: Reproducible Benchmarks and Physics-Informed Evaluation for Powder Diffraction Symmetry Classification
papers.abstract: Machine learning for powder diffraction (PXRD) symmetry classification is being trained at scale, yet the field lacks a common evaluation standard: papers report results on different subsets of experimental archives, with different target taxonomies, preprocessing, and metrics, and published models are rarely released in a form that permits rescoring. We present InformedXRD, an evaluation framework with three parts: (i) a machine-readable mapping from 230 space groups to 99 extinction groups, the finest classes powder diffraction can identify from systematic absences alone; (ii) a benchmark-construction method whose inclusion rules are specified as code and reproduce from a frozen snapshot, instantiated as RRUFF-473, RRUFF-325, and, as a small example, opXRD-98; (iii) a reporting protocol with prior-only frequency baselines, a label-permutation test, a hierarchy-aware error metric on the condensed translationengleiche subgroup graph, and stratified evaluation. We build on the mapping, RRUFF benchmarks, subgroup graph, and four ViT checkpoints released in our earlier work (Baggett et al., 2026). Using these checkpoints, a 1D residual CNN, and six architectures trained under the XRDBench recipe (Cao et al., 2025), we show that evaluation design changes what conclusions are justified: paired tests point in different directions at Top-1 and Top-5; paired Top-k tests do not separate the three leading XRDBench models, while hierarchy-aware analysis describes error distance and direction across all six; an input-blind frequency predictor matches the models on aggregate Top-k, yet a label-permutation test still detects pattern-specific evidence; and stratified analysis exposes a label-entropy confound that aggregate accuracy hides. All mapping tables, benchmark code, scripts, and checkpoints are released as shared infrastructure for PXRD-ML evaluation.

papers.title: OpenULF: A Modular Toolkit Enables Data-Driven Ultra-Low-Field MRI with both Classical and Quantum Sensors
papers.abstract: Ultra-low-field (ULF) Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) offers a portable, low-cost alternative to conventional scanners by operating at field strengths below 10 mT. At these fields, two sensor technologies compete: quantum SQUID (Superconducting Quantum Interference Device) sensors, which provide high sensitivity but require cryogenic cooling, and classical induction coils, which are inexpensive and room-temperature but produce weaker signals. With conventional physics-based imaging, both suffer from low signal-to-noise ratios (SNR). Data-driven reconstruction has overcome similar limits in related inverse problems, but its use for ULF-MRI has been hindered by a lack of open datasets, benchmarks, and flexible simulators. To close this gap, we present OpenULF, a modular, open-source simulation toolkit that generates paired training data and supports end-to-end machine-learning (ML) reconstruction. OpenULF integrates a Bloch-equation-validated physics simulator, calibrated SQUID and coil receiver models, reconstruction ML networks, and an automated design-space exploration engine. Architecturally, a receiver abstract base class, a typed HDF5 contract that decouples physics from learning, and a resumable sweep engine make sensors, models, and datasets independently substitutable. Using OpenULF, we train 774 models across four anatomical datasets and conduct three design-space explorations. The effectiveness of ML reconstruction depends strongly on the dataset and the sensor. We identify a SQUID-to-coil crossover near 450 $μ$T and demonstrate that sensor hardware and ML model capacity can be traded off during system design. Sensor and reconstruction choices must therefore be co-designed: the best sensor is set by the dataset and field strength, not by SNR.

papers.title: A Debiased Machine Learning Single-Imputation Framework for Item Nonresponse in Surveys
papers.abstract: Machine-learning methods offer flexible alternatives to parametric models for imputing missing survey values. However, using their predictions in the customary imputed estimator does not automatically yield valid inference. We explain why the error from estimating the regression function can prevent root-$n$ consistency and develop inference for a finite population mean using a cross-fitted augmented inverse-probability-weighted (AIPW) estimator. The analysis combines an imputation model, a sampling design, and a missing-at-random response mechanism, while allowing dependence among sampling indicators. We establish double robustness and show that, under suitable regularity conditions, consistency of both nuisance estimators together with a product-rate condition yields oracle equivalence and asymptotic normality. We also derive consistent variance estimators accounting for sampling and nonresponse. To obtain a completed survey variable, we construct adjusted imputed values that preserve observed responses and whose weighted mean reproduces the AIPW estimate exactly. We further discuss aggregation of nuisance learners and the conditions under which it preserves the prediction rates needed for inference. Simulations show that cross-fitting can substantially reduce undercoverage, but may increase mean squared error when nuisance predictions are inaccurate.

papers.title: The Stability of Data Exchange in Competitive Markets
papers.abstract: We study the stability of data exchange among competing firms. Unlike tangible goods, data is non-rival: sharing it does not deprive the giver of its use. On one hand, competing firms-- often operating as machine-learning-driven predictors that collect observations from a shared environment to solve similar tasks-- can improve their predictive accuracies from pooling data. On the other hand, they compete for market share, which may depend on their relative predictive performance. This raises the central question of this paper: can there be a stable data exchange in such competitive environments?   We formalize this via a model of $n$ firms exchanging fractions of their datasets, with predictive performance feeding into market competition. We adopt core stability as our solution concept, accounting for externalities via worst-case responses by non-participating firms. Our main results reveal a sharp contrast driven by demand structure: (i) in fully rational markets, where customers flock entirely to the top-performing firm, a core-stable exchange always exists for any monotone continuous prediction functions; (ii) in partially rational markets with logit-style demand, core-stable exchanges may fail to exist-and even approximate cores can be empty. Our impossibility results suggest that internal profit-sharing within coalitions can restore stability in partially rational markets. We formalize this intuition by showing that when co-operating coalitions equally redistribute market-share revenues among members, a core-stable data exchange exists. Finally, we propose a natural exchange dynamic and demonstrate empirically that it converges to a core-stable data exchange in fully rational markets on simulated instances derived from real datasets.

papers.title: Boson sampling is fragile to loss
papers.abstract: Boson sampling experiments aim to demonstrate quantum computational advantage with increasing numbers of interfering photons. A central question is whether their computational hardness survives under photon loss. We show that even an arbitrarily small nonzero uniform loss rate permits efficient classical sampling in the average case when the rate remains fixed as the system grows. We exploit how loss suppresses correlations involving many photons to approximate the full output distribution using low correlation orders. The resulting samplers run in time polynomial in system size and inverse total variation error, with the error averaged over Haar random interferometers. The results apply to Fock state boson sampling with single-photon states in distinct input modes and arbitrary additional vacuum inputs, and to Gaussian boson sampling with equal squeezing of bounded strength in every input mode. Classical sampling is efficient even when the mean detected photon number grows linearly with system size, showing that large photon counts alone do not ensure computational hardness.
